name: SplashLearn
line: SplashLearn teaches in games with rewards, to grade 5. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs SplashLearn: SplashLearn teaches in games with rewards, to grade 5. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: SplashLearn teaches preschool to grade 5 math through game-based activities with rewards [3], along a personalized learning path [4][6], and reviews past topics in a live class once a month [7]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, each problem carries what a learner needs: a hint that gives the first step and never the answer, a written lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer after it is answered, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In SplashLearn the unit is the game-based activity, which earns rewards [1][3]. Teachers assign lessons [4][6]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [11].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. SplashLearn runs a live class once a month, the Monthly Mash-up, in which a teacher reviews the past month's topics [7]. We found no scheduled review of earlier skills inside its practice on the pages we read [3][5][6]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [12].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math and runs from counting through precalculus in one program. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. SplashLearn says its practice adapts to each student's level along a personalized learning path [4][6]. Its math runs from preschool through grade 5 [1][3].

reasons.title: The adult does not plan
reasons.body: In AMP the adult does not plan, teach or grade. Parents and teachers see a level for each part of math and the actual problems behind every number, and each lesson has a guide for the adult. In SplashLearn, teachers assign lessons and read color-coded reports [4][6]. Its homeschool page presents it as flexible enough to fit a family's own lesson plans, with weekly progress reports [5].

rows.range: Preschool, ages 2 to 5, through grade 5, in math and English [1][3].

theirs: SplashLearn is a game-based learning program in math and English for preschool through grade 5, on the web and in apps [1]. Its math is aligned to the Common Core, and activities are tagged with standards such as 3.NF.1 [3]. It also offers printable worksheets and lesson plans [1][3].

Children practice through game-based activities that earn rewards [3]. SplashLearn says the practice adapts to each child's level along a personalized learning path, and teachers can assign lessons and read reports [4][6]. A live class each month, the Monthly Mash-up, reviews the past month's topics with a teacher [7].
credit: Math practice in game form, from preschool age [1][3].
Each activity is tagged with the standard it teaches [3].
A teacher returns to the past month's topics in a live class [7].

theirs: SplashLearn's efficacy page says it meets the ESSA Tier 3 evidence standard [2]. The study behind that claim, described in a July 2025 company blog post, used 2023-24 data from kindergarten to grade 5 in one North Carolina public school district. SplashLearn ran it with Instructure and the International Centre for EdTech Impact, with support from the Jacobs Foundation [8].

The design is correlational. Students who solved more problems each week ended with higher mastery scores, especially in kindergarten to grade 4, after controlling for where they started. Mastery was measured by SplashLearn's own in-app assessment, not an outside test. The post gives no sample size and no effect size, and describes no comparison group that did not use SplashLearn [8]. Students who practice most each week often differ from the rest before they start.

Evidence for ESSA lists Splash Math, which we take to be SplashLearn's earlier name, without a rating: "No studies met inclusion requirements" [9]. The page names no provider [9]. We found no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report on it in our check [10].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Worked examples improve mathematics performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 across 55 studies [11]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed, spaced practice scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks, on the researchers' own test a month later [12]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child is young and practices most when math comes as a game.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in ordinary practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or past grade 5.
You want the program to plan, teach and check the math, and to show you the problems behind every number.

questions.question: How is AMP different from SplashLearn?
questions.answer: SplashLearn teaches preschool to grade 5 math in game-based activities with rewards, along a personalized learning path [3][4]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does SplashLearn work?
questions.answer: Its one study is correlational: students who solved more problems each week ended with higher mastery scores on SplashLearn's own assessment. It reports no effect size and no comparison group [8]. Evidence for ESSA lists Splash Math, likely its earlier name, without a rating [9].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers and chooses practice from there.
